issues.detail: Error handling is thin: the fetch helpers never check HTTP status, GraphQL top-level errors, rate limits or throttling, and webhook setup and HMAC verification are not covered even though Example 2 relies on them.

The three examples are only a user prompt and a one-line description of what the agent will do, with no concrete code or output, and Examples 2 and 3 are not backed by runnable code in the skill, such as webhook handling or cartCreate.

scenarios.name: staff-editable-hero-section
scenarios.rationale: Both supply a section file with a schema (image_picker, text, richtext, url), a preset, section.settings.* reads, a blank check guarding the button, and image_url: width:; Response B reads more fully as a finished section because it adds responsive image_tag output, a placeholder fallback and style controls, while Response A is simpler but fully meets the core rubric.

scenarios.name: admin-api-create-product
scenarios.rationale: Both pin the API version, use X-Shopify-Access-Token, select userErrors, call publishablePublish and read the admin token from an environment variable, but A uses the rubric's productCreate mutation with ProductCreateInput while B uses productSet with ProductSetInput, which the rubric doesn't allow; A also states that productCreate leaves the product unpublished, while B explains the same point less directly and verifies more thoroughly.

scenarios.name: headless-cart-checkout-flow
scenarios.rationale: Both meet every rubric item: POST to the Storefront endpoint with a pinned API version and the token header, products queried with edges/node (A) or nodes (B), cartCreate with merchandiseId and quantity lines, redirect to cart.checkoutUrl, and no legacy Checkout mutations. A follows the rubric's edges/node structure literally, while B uses the `nodes` shorthand and adds a more complete cart (update, fragments, context) plus useful notes, so B is slightly ahead on depth and A slightly ahead on literal match.
